$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/ee/eed043488a6cd3949da95907125dcdfa2f946feefff60772495e48e9610c4bc1.png)

Now, since

$$
P(x,y)=e^{-x^2}-x^2y,\quad Q(x,y)=y+xy^2,
$$

we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=- x^{2},\quad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C(e^{-x^2}-x^2y)\,dx+(y+xy^2)\,dy&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\ &=\iint_D\left(y^{2}-(- x^{2})\right)\,dA \\ &=\iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 1,0\le\theta\le 2 \pi\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA&=\iint_\Delta (r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta))\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{1}r^3(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{1}r^3\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{1}\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left(\frac{1}{4}-0\right)\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\frac{1}{4}\,d\theta \\ &=\frac{1}{4}[\theta]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ &=\frac{1}{4}\left(2 \pi-0\right) \\ &=\frac{\pi}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\iint_D 4(x^2+y^2)\,dA&=\iint_\Delta 4(r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta))\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=4\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{2}r^3(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=4\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{2}r^3\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=4\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{2}\,d\theta \\ &=4\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left(4-0\right)\,d\theta \\ &=4\int_{0}^{2 \pi}4\,d\theta \\ &=16[\theta]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ &=16\left(2 \pi-0\right) \\ &=32 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate $\oint_C(\sqrt{5+x}-5x^2y)\,dx+(e^{-y^2}+5xy^2)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/3b/3ba969ce97031cecfc6c60ce908a082b268c11a474e6a588b9719ef2ce39e0d2.png)

Now, since

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{5+x}-5x^2y,\quad Q(x,y)=e^{-y^2}+5xy^2,
$$

we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=- 5 x^{2},\quad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=5 y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C(\sqrt{5+x}-5x^2y)\,dx+(e^{-y^2}+5xy^2)\,dy&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\ &=\iint_D\left(5 y^{2}-(- 5 x^{2})\right)\,dA \\ &=\iint_D 5(x^2+y^2)\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):1\le r\le 2,0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D 5(x^2+y^2)\,dA&=\iint_\Delta 5(r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta))\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=5\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{1}^{2}r^3(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=5\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{1}^{2}r^3\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=5\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{1}^{2}\,d\theta \\ &=5\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(4-\frac{1}{4}\right)\,d\theta \\ &=5\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{15}{4}\,d\theta \\ &=\frac{75}{4}[\theta]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &=\frac{75}{4}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-0\right) \\ &=\frac{75 \pi}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Now, since

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{x+1}-x^2y,\quad Q(x,y)=e^y+xy^2,
$$

we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=- x^{2},\quad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C(\sqrt{x+1}-x^2y)\,dx+(e^y+xy^2)\,dy&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\ &=\iint_D\left(y^{2}-(- x^{2})\right)\,dA \\ &=\iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 4,0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.
$$

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA&=\iint_\Delta (r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta))\,r\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{4}r^3(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{4}r^3\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left[\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{4}\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(64-0\right)\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}64\,d\theta \\ &=64[\theta]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &=64\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-0\right) \\ &=32 \pi.\end{aligned}
